tldr: To avoid the heavy computational cost of high-fidelity physics simulators, this paper builds neural reduced dynamics (NRD) models that retain only the physical quantities essential for control. Training reinforcement learning policies in these tens-of-thousands-of-times faster environments enables successful zero-shot transfer back to high-fidelity simulators.
overview:
Controlling complex robots or vehicles on off-road terrain using reinforcement learning requires millions of trial-and-error steps. However, high-fidelity physics simulators like Project Chrono, while faithfully reproducing soil deformation and intricate multibody contacts, are computationally very heavy and run many times slower than real time, making direct reinforcement learning impractical.

While one might think of building a neural network surrogate of the physics dynamics, learning the entire simulator state directly is difficult. Conversely, oversimplifying the model strips away essential control physics like tire slip and load transfer. To tackle this challenge, the authors propose a design principle called Neural Reduced Dynamics (NRD): retain only the phenomena necessary for control, and move anything that can be computed analytically outside the model.

Specifically, based on data collected from a high-fidelity simulator, a causal transformer learns the transitions of a task-relevant reduced state. The trained model is then parallelized across thousands of instances on a single GPU to train policies with PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization), which are ultimately evaluated closed-loop back in the original high-fidelity simulator. The authors validate this across two case studies: a High-Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle (HMMWV) traversing off-road terrain including deformable soil, and a tracked vehicle with a front-mounted articulated arm.

As a result, the NRD models achieve up to roughly 58,400x faster simulation speed compared to the high-fidelity simulator, making policy learning practical in a short amount of time. Furthermore, a single policy trained purely inside the NRD environment achieves higher tracking accuracy than single-terrain specialists across rigid flat, deformable soil, and zero-shot bumpy terrains in the high-fidelity simulator, while the tracked vehicle and arm demonstrate extremely high goal-reaching rates without any collisions or joint-limit violations.
contributions: Established a neural reduced dynamics (NRD) design framework that selects task-relevant control states, separates analytical kinematic calculations and external context, and enables parallelized training.

Achieved zero-shot, superior tracking performance across all environments—including unlearned bumpy terrain—using a single generalist policy with a 15-dimensional abstraction incorporating rigid/deformable soil context, wheel normal forces, and wheel speeds.

Learned control policies that reliably transfer back to a high-fidelity simulator from the same framework across two distinct subsystems: a tracked vehicle (3D state) and a 4-DoF articulated arm (8D state).
Achieved up to roughly 58,400x higher simulation throughput compared to the high-fidelity simulator, enabling reinforcement learning iterations within practical timeframes.

sections.heading: Finding the 'Right Abstraction' to Bridge High-Fidelity Physics and RL
sections.summary: While high-fidelity simulators are indispensable for evaluating complex robots, they are far too slow for iterative reinforcement learning. This work proposes an NRD framework that extracts only the control-relevant physics, reconciling ultra-fast RL with reliable policy transfer to high-fidelity environments.
sections.details:
Vehicles traversing soft terrain, tracked robots, and articulated arms are governed by complex physics such as friction and deformable contact that are difficult to write down compactly in closed-form equations. High-fidelity simulators like Project Chrono faithfully reproduce these phenomena, but they run many times slower than real time. Because reinforcement learning demands millions of interaction steps, training policies directly in such high-fidelity environments is practically infeasible.

Neural dynamics surrogates are a common alternative, but they face the core dilemma of what to model and what to discard. Learning the entire simulator state is intractable due to high dimensionality. On the other hand, oversimplifying ignores critical control physics like tire slip, load transfer, and actuator response lags, causing learned policies to fail in high-fidelity environments. Furthermore, small one-step prediction errors alone do not guarantee a viable RL environment, as errors compound quickly over long rollouts.

To address this, the authors propose the NRD framework, which preserves task-relevant fidelity rather than simply reducing state dimensions. Using data collected from the simulator, a causal transformer learns only the state transitions essential for the task, while quantities like global pose and forward-kinematic end-effector positions are computed analytically outside the model. This frozen model is then parallelized across thousands of instances on a GPU to train policies with PPO, which are finally validated closed-loop back in Chrono. The core insight lies in organizing what to propagate as state, what to provide as input, and what to recover analytically outside the model.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of World Models, Model Reduction, and Terramechanics
sections.summary: This work combines insights from learned dynamics models, projection-based model order reduction, and terramechanics simulation. Unlike world models that learn full latent representations end-to-end, it directly selects physically meaningful variables and couples them with external analytical computation.
sections.details:
To clarify the positioning of this research, it helps to distinguish it from related fields:

### Learned Dynamics Models and World Models
Model-based RL methods like PETS and MBPO use predictive models to reduce data collection costs in real environments. However, when running entire episodes purely inside a surrogate model—as done here—autoregressive error accumulation becomes a severe challenge. Additionally, while latent world models like World Models and Dreamer discover latent spaces end-to-end from high-dimensional observations such as images, this work starts with known physical quantities (velocities, normal forces, etc.) from the simulator. The central focus is variable selection and validation: deciding which physically meaningful variables to retain and which to drop.

### Model Order Reduction (ROM) and Structured Models
In physics simulation, model order reduction (ROM) has long been studied to accelerate computation by projecting systems onto lower-dimensional subspaces. This work builds on that philosophy, but instead of using black-box compressors, it reduces dimensionality based on domain knowledge while preserving physical meaning. Quantities whose dynamics are invariant and can simply be integrated later, such as global position and heading, are intentionally excluded from model predictions and recovered analytically.

### High-Fidelity Simulators and Context-Conditioned Models
Popular robot learning simulators like Isaac Lab and MuJoCo excel at massive parallelization, but they have limitations when it comes to faithful terramechanics (soft soil mechanics) and detailed vehicle suspensions. Therefore, this study adopts Chrono as the ground-truth reference physics. Furthermore, because vehicle behavior changes drastically between rigid and soft soil for the exact same control action, the authors supply explicit context signals (labels) to the model to resolve dynamics ambiguity.

sections.heading: NRD Design Principles: What to Predict, What to Input, and What to Solve Analytically
sections.summary: The NRD framework partitions simulator information into four categories: recurrent state, control actions, operating context, and analytically recovered quantities. Models are selected based on long rollout errors rather than one-step errors, and parallelized on GPUs for RL training.
sections.details:
The overall pipeline and design rules of the NRD framework are as follows:

### 3.1 Reduced Dynamics Formulation
For high-fidelity simulator state $x_t$, a task-specific reduced projection $z_t = P(x_t)$ is defined. The NRD model $f_\theta$ takes a history of $k$ past reduced states $z_{t-k:t}$, control commands $a_{t-k:t}$, and operational context $c_{t-k:t}$, and autoregressively predicts the next state increment $\Delta \hat{z}_t$ (with $\hat{z}_{t+1} = \hat{z}_t + \Delta \hat{z}_t$).
A key principle here is the four-way partition of information:
- **Recurrent state $z_t$**: Physical quantities dependent on uncertainty and contact, which the model must learn to update.
- **Action $a_t$**: Control commands supplied externally.
- **Context $c_t$**: Mode information (e.g., ground conditions) that resolves ambiguities where the same state and action would otherwise yield different next states.
- **Analytically recovered quantities $y_t = G(\hat{z}_{\le t})$**: Quantities that can be uniquely calculated from predicted states via known kinematics (e.g., pose integrated from vehicle speed, or end-effector position from joint angles). These are kept outside the model and computed analytically.

### 3.2 Abstraction Rules and Network Architecture
The criterion for state selection is control relevance: does changing this variable alter the controller's decision? Invariant quantities, such as absolute coordinates on flat ground, are excluded. The model architecture uses a GPT-style causal transformer with self-attention over history sequences. The attention mechanism captures actuator delays and contact history effects that instantaneous values alone cannot convey.

### 3.3 Training and Model Selection
Models are trained via supervised learning (e.g., Huber loss) on diverse excitation driving data collected from Chrono. Crucially, models are never selected based on one-step validation loss. Because models with good one-step predictions often drift during long autoregressive rollouts, checkpoints are selected based on minimum long-rollout error on unseen evaluation episodes.

### 3.4 Policy Learning and Tiered Validation
The selected NRD model has its parameters frozen and is parallelized across thousands of environments on a single GPU for PPO training. The policy observes only the states predicted by NRD and their analytically recovered quantities to choose actions. Validation proceeds through three tiers: one-step accuracy $\rightarrow$ open-loop long-rollout accuracy $\rightarrow$ closed-loop transfer in Chrono, where final control success in the real Chrono environment serves as the decisive metric.

sections.heading: Case Study 1: Wheeled Vehicle Trajectory Tracking from Soft Soil to Unseen Bumps
sections.summary: Using a military HMMWV, trajectory tracking across rigid flat ground and SPH-based Continuum Representation Model (CRM) deformable soil was evaluated. A single generalist policy with a 15D state including normal forces, wheel speeds, and terrain context achieved the best performance across all environments, including zero-shot bumpy terrain.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Target System and Task Setup
The study used Chrono's detailed HMMWV model, featuring all-wheel drive, an automatic transmission, and full suspension kinematics. Three evaluation terrains were prepared: (1) rigid flat ground, (2) deformable soil modeled via the SPH (Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics)-based Continuum Representation Model (CRM), and (3) an unseen bumpy rigid terrain never presented during training. Resolving over 14 million SPH particles makes CRM soil simulation tens of times more expensive than rigid flat ground.

### 4.2 15-Dimensional Reduced State and Terramechanics
The chosen reduced state $z$ contains 15 dimensions:
- Base vehicle motion (7D): planar velocities $v_x, v_y$, attitude angles (roll $\phi$, pitch $\theta$), and 3-axis angular velocities $\omega_x, \omega_y, \omega_z$
- Terramechanics block (8D): four-wheel normal forces $F_z^{(i)}$ and four-wheel rotational speeds $\omega^{(i)}$

Why are normal forces and wheel speeds required? On soft soil, applying wheel torque causes tires to slip, with slip ratios ($s \approx 1 - v_x / (\omega r)$) approaching 25% alongside body sinkage. Without both chassis velocity and wheel speed, slip cannot be captured; without normal forces, load transfer during cornering, braking, and acceleration cannot be represented. Global pose $(x, y, \psi)$ is omitted from the model and reconstructed by integrating velocity and yaw rate.

### 4.3 Terrain Context and Training
Identical throttle inputs produce vastly different vehicle responses on flat ground versus CRM soil. To resolve this transition ambiguity, a 2D one-hot context token was appended to input tokens: $[1, 0]$ for flat ground and $[0, 1]$ for CRM. The model is an 8-layer causal transformer (6.4M parameters). Training data from flat ground and CRM were sampled in a 75:25 ratio and optimized with a domain-reweighted Huber loss to prevent high-variance CRM force signals from dominating.

### 4.4 Open-Loop Dynamics Model Evaluation
A model trained only on flat ground saw its rollout error explode to 194% on CRM, while a CRM-only model had a 40% error on flat ground. In contrast, the context-conditioned generalist model maintained rollout errors of 3.7% on flat ground and 5.4% on CRM, matching the high long-term predictive accuracy of the respective specialists.

### 4.5 RL Tracking Control and Transfer to Chrono
The frozen generalist NRD model was parallelized across 2,048 environments to train a trajectory tracking policy with PPO. Notably, terrain context was intentionally omitted from policy observations, which received only state history and target path information. When this single generalist policy was deployed back into the high-fidelity Chrono environment, it produced striking results:
- **Flat ground**: Median tracking error of 0.157 m for the generalist policy (vs. 0.174 m for the flat specialist).
- **CRM deformable soil**: Median tracking error of 0.180 m for the generalist policy (vs. 0.231 m for the CRM specialist).
- **Unseen bumpy terrain**: Median tracking error of 0.149 m for the generalist policy (vs. 0.187 m for the flat specialist and 0.213 m for the CRM specialist).

The generalist policy outperformed both specialists on their home turfs as well as across terrains. It also demonstrated robust zero-shot tracking on bumpy terrain that was never seen during training.

sections.heading: Case Study 2: Disentangling Tracked Vehicle Mobility and 4-DoF Arm Reaching
sections.summary: For an M113 tracked vehicle equipped with a front-mounted 4-DoF arm, two distinct abstractions were applied: drive mode (3D state) and arm reaching mode (8D state). Policies trained inside NRD achieved a 100% vehicle goal-reaching rate and a 97% arm goal-reaching rate in the high-fidelity Chrono environment.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Platform and Dual Operating Modes
Case Study II considers a complex robotic system: an M113 tracked vehicle with over 150 degrees of freedom and numerous track shoes, equipped with a 4-DoF articulated arm on its front chassis. Two independent modes were defined for this system:
- **Drive mode**: With the arm locked in its home pose, the vehicle navigates to planar goals 20–40 m away.
- **Reach mode**: With the vehicle stationary, the arm end-effector reaches toward 3D target coordinates.

Running this composite system in Chrono achieves only 0.28x real time, but replacing it with NRD models accelerates RL training by thousands to tens of thousands of times.

### 5.2 Abstraction Design Tailored to Each Task
- **Tracked vehicle abstraction**: The state is 3-dimensional, consisting solely of body-frame velocities and yaw rate $z^{\mathrm{veh}} = [v_x, v_y, r]$. All 154 rigid bodies and track shoe interactions are discarded, modeling only the planar motion needed for control. Global pose $(x, y, \psi)$ is integrated outside the model.
- **Articulated arm abstraction**: The state is 8-dimensional, comprising joint angles and joint velocities $z^{\mathrm{arm}} = [q, \dot{q}]$. End-effector position $p^{\mathrm{ee}}$ is not learned; it is computed analytically via forward kinematics (FK). Unlike vehicle position, arm joint angles $q$ directly dictate gravity torques and joint limits, making it essential to keep them as recurrent states rather than integrating from velocities (an ablation integrating from velocities worsened error by nearly 30x).

### 5.3 Model Training and Accuracy
The vehicle model used a 3-layer transformer (0.34M parameters), while the arm model used a 5-layer transformer (4.0M parameters). Over a 5-second open-loop rollout, the vehicle model achieved a distance-normalized error of just 5.85%, while the arm end-effector rollout error over 2 seconds was only about 1.2%.

### 5.4 PPO Training Inside Frozen NRD Models
- **Vehicle goal reaching**: Trained with PPO across 2,048 parallel NRD environments, reaching a 100% success rate in approximately 10 minutes of wall-clock time.
- **Arm reaching control**: Trained across 4,096 parallel environments. To prevent the arm from colliding with the ground or vehicle chassis, a GPU-parallel FK-based geometric 'safety shield' was introduced. Hazardous commands were filtered out, and clearance distances were provided to the policy as observations. The policy converged in roughly 57 minutes.

### 5.5 Closed-Loop Transfer to Chrono
The learned policies were deployed into the high-fidelity Chrono environment and rigorously evaluated on 100 fixed-seed test targets.
- **Vehicle**: With an acceptance threshold of 0.75 m, it succeeded on 100 out of 100 targets (median closest distance of 0.691 m, median arrival time of 20.2 seconds). For targets located behind it, the vehicle executed smooth U-turns resembling forward driving rather than pure pivot turns, generating efficient trajectories.
- **Arm**: With a tight threshold of 0.05 m (5 cm), it succeeded on 97 out of 100 targets (median error of 4.2 cm, convergence time of 0.9 seconds). The 3 failed attempts were timeouts in deep, lower regions of the workspace with sparse training coverage. Across all trials, there were zero collisions with the chassis or ground and zero joint-limit violations.

sections.heading: Four Core Principles for Control-Oriented Model Reduction
sections.summary: Across both case studies, four common design principles emerge for effective surrogate models: aligning state selection with dominant physics, moving analytical computation outside the model, resolving ambiguity with context, and accelerating iteration through high throughput.
sections.details:
Lessons drawn from the experiments on 'learning the right abstraction' synthesize into four core principles:

### 6.1 Abstraction Follows Task and Dominant Physics
For the HMMWV, tire-soil interactions (load transfer and slip) were dominant, so normal forces and wheel speeds were included in the state. For the tracked vehicle's planar navigation, three chassis velocity components were sufficient, whereas the arm required joint angles and velocities to capture nonlinear joint torques. There is no universal reduced state; state design must reflect the dominant physical phenomena governing the task.

### 6.2 Learn Only Uncertain Transitions; Solve Known Structure Analytically
Global vehicle pose can be integrated from body velocities, and arm end-effector positions and collision clearances are computed exactly via forward kinematics. Leaving these analytical computations outside the neural network saves model parameters and enforces geometric consistency, preventing model breakdowns.

### 6.3 Resolve Physical Ambiguities Arising from Reduction with Context
Aggressive state reduction can introduce one-to-many ambiguities where identical states and actions yield different outcomes across physical environments (e.g., rigid ground vs. mud). Rather than forcing the network to infer this implicitly from history, providing explicit low-dimensional context labels (such as one-hot vectors) dramatically suppresses long-term model drift.

### 6.4 High Throughput Enables Practical RL Iteration
NRD models run thousands to tens of thousands of times faster than Chrono. Real-world RL success relies heavily on human-in-the-loop tuning of reward weights and regularization terms. When training takes hours or days, rapid iteration is impossible; by reducing training time to 10–60 minutes on a GPU, practical controllers can be engineered rapidly.

sections.heading: Limitations: Sim-to-Real Gap and Manual Abstraction Design
sections.summary: This study is limited to simulation-to-simulation (Sim-to-Sim) transfer and does not address transfer to physical hardware (Sim-to-Real) or raw sensor inputs like camera streams. Furthermore, abstraction rules rely on human physical insight, and handling abrupt contact mode changes remains an open challenge.
sections.details:
The authors highlight several limitations and directions for future research:

- **Sim-to-Sim limitation**: Validation is performed entirely within Chrono; real-robot transfer (Sim-to-Real) is not demonstrated. The surrogate models may inherit internal modeling biases present in Chrono.
- **Reliance on privileged simulator states**: The framework assumes direct access to simulator states like wheel speeds, normal forces, and exact joint angles, without addressing sensor noise, state estimation errors, or end-to-end learning from camera images.
- **Manual abstraction engineering**: Selecting which variables to retain and which context tokens to introduce depends on researcher physical insight and trial-and-error. Automating this process via algorithmic state-space discovery remains an open goal.
- **Discontinuous contact mode switches**: The arm validation was restricted to free-space motion. Handling abrupt, multi-modal contact events such as grasping, object impacts, and tool interactions remains an unresolved challenge.

sections.heading: A Bridge Between Accurate Physics Simulation and Scalable Robot Learning
sections.summary: Designing task-tailored neural reduced dynamics accelerates simulation by roughly four orders of magnitude while preserving physical fidelity, enabling high-throughput policy learning and reliable transfer to high-fidelity environments. It offers a practical bridge across the simulation-learning divide.
sections.details:
This paper presents a framework for extracting task-specific neural reduced dynamics (NRD) from high-fidelity robot simulators and using them as massively parallel RL training environments. The core insight is that model reduction should not merely compress state vectors, but select the 'right abstraction': preserving the physics critical to control while computing known kinematics analytically outside the model.

Across three distinct control tasks—an off-road wheeled vehicle, a tracked platform, and an articulated arm—policies trained entirely within frozen NRD models transferred closed-loop back to the Chrono high-fidelity simulator. By accelerating simulation speeds by up to roughly 58,400x, this approach provides a scalable and practical bridge connecting computationally heavy, high-fidelity physics engines with data-hungry robot reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Speed Benchmarks and Detailed Ablation Findings
sections.summary: The appendix details computational throughput measurements reaching up to 58,400x, causal transformer architectural sweeps, data scaling laws, and comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating the necessity of specific state variables and context tokens.
sections.details:
Key takeaways from the detailed experimental data reported in the appendix include:

### Computational Throughput (Appendix A)
Comparing the Real-Time Factor (RTF: simulated seconds per real-time second), Chrono achieved 0.152x on CRM deformable soil (roughly 6.6x slower than real time) and 0.279x on the tracked vehicle with arm. In contrast, batched NRD models running on a single GPU reached approximately 1,750x RTF for the HMMWV, 16,300x RTF for the tracked vehicle, and 2,320x RTF for the arm. Compared to a single Chrono process, the speedup ratio reached roughly 11,500x on CRM soil, 58,400x on the tracked vehicle, and 8,300x on the arm.

### Validation via Ablation Studies (Appendix E)
Ablations confirm why the 15D state and context tokens were necessary:
- **Removing one-hot context**: While one-step validation loss barely changed, open-loop long-rollout error on flat ground more than doubled, increasing from 3.73% to 8.26%. This confirms that history sequences alone cannot fully disambiguate ground properties.
- **Removing terramechanics (normal forces and wheel speeds)**: Flat-ground error remained steady, but rollout error on CRM deformable soil jumped from 5.38% to 8.00% (a ~49% increase) due to the model's inability to represent tire slip.

### Transformer Architecture and Data Scaling (Appendices C & D)
Architectural sweeps revealed that layer depth is the most critical parameter, with performance plateauing around 8 layers. Furthermore, rollout errors decreased monotonically as training data increased from 20% to 80%, confirming that scaling laws observed in modern transformer models also hold for surrogate robot dynamics.

takeaways: When building surrogate models for reinforcement learning, do not predict full simulator states; retain only control-relevant physical quantities in the recurrent state and compute analytically tractable quantities (like pose and end-effector coordinates) outside the model.
Never use one-step prediction loss for model selection; checkpoint selection must be based on autoregressive long-rollout errors, such as distance-normalized error.

When differing operating environments yield divergent transitions from identical states and actions, provide explicit context labels rather than relying on implicit history inference to suppress long-term rollout drift.
Achieving thousands-of-times speedups with GPU-parallelized surrogates enables multiple RL reward and hyperparameter iterations per day, making practical policy discovery drastically easier.
limitations: Evaluation is restricted to Sim-to-Sim transfer (from Chrono to NRD and back to Chrono); Sim-to-Real transfer under hardware noise and unmodeled real-world effects remains unverified.
The approach assumes direct access to privileged simulator states such as tire normal forces and joint velocities, omitting state estimation from raw sensor data like onboard cameras.
Reduced state abstraction rules rely on human physical insight, requiring manual task-by-task engineering and trial-and-error for each new robotic system.
Discontinuous contact dynamics—such as manipulation, collision, and sudden contact mode transitions—are omitted, limiting current validation to free-space arm motions.
